topic: How Fast Can an Arcade Machine Pay for Itself in a Bar or Event Venue?
dominant_search_intent: [MOCK] Commercial investigation with a strong transactional undertone — searchers are bar owners, venue managers, or aspiring operators trying to decide whether an arcade machine purchase or placement deal is financially justified before committing capital.
common_angles: [MOCK] Vendor and distributor sales pages framing arcade machines as a 'passive income' or 'low-effort revenue stream' for bar owners
[MOCK] Operator forum threads (arcade/vending/route operator communities) trading anecdotal weekly earnings figures with heavy variance and no methodology
[MOCK] Generic 'how much does an arcade machine make' listicles that cite vague industry ranges without showing the underlying math
[MOCK] Revenue-split explainer content aimed at route operators negotiating placement deals with venue owners, rather than at the venue owner's own investment decision
[MOCK] Coin-op and amusement industry trade content that assumes B2B operator knowledge and skips basic definitions a first-time buyer would need
common_sections: [MOCK] How much can you make with an arcade machine (single blended average figure, no scenario range)
[MOCK] Best types of arcade machines/games for bars
[MOCK] Revenue split between venue and machine owner
[MOCK] Where to place the machine for maximum earnings
[MOCK] Buy vs lease vs revenue-share placement comparison
[MOCK] Generic call to action to contact a distributor or route operator
competitor_strengths: [MOCK] Route-operator-facing content is usually detailed and credible on how revenue-split deals are structured in practice
[MOCK] Some vendor pages give concrete example machine prices, which helps ground reader expectations
[MOCK] Placement and foot-traffic advice (where in the venue to put the machine) tends to be practical and experience-based
competitor_weaknesses: [MOCK] Weekly or monthly earnings figures are usually presented as a single confident number with no stated assumptions, making them unverifiable and often misleading
[MOCK] Almost no ranking content separates the payback period from the ongoing profit that follows it — the two get blurred into one vague 'ROI' claim
[MOCK] Best-case anecdotes from high-traffic venues are frequently presented as typical, inflating reader expectations
[MOCK] Maintenance costs and electricity costs are rarely quantified at all, let alone subtracted from revenue before an ROI claim is made
[MOCK] Seasonality and slow-venue variance are mentioned only in passing, if at all, despite being a major driver of real-world payback timelines
[MOCK] Content is written for operators already in the amusement business, not for a venue owner evaluating a first-time purchase decision from scratch
content_gaps: [MOCK] No transparent, checkable multi-scenario model (pessimistic / base case / optimistic) with stated assumptions the reader can re-run with their own numbers
[MOCK] No clear treatment of what happens after payback — the ongoing net monthly profit once the machine has paid for itself is essentially absent from ranking content
[MOCK] No honest discussion of how probable each earnings scenario actually is, versus presenting all outcomes as equally likely
[MOCK] No worked example tying a real, named list price to a full weekly-to-monthly-to-annual calculation a skeptical reader could verify line by line
[MOCK] No content distinguishing home-leisure buyers who host events at a secondary property from full-time commercial bar operators, despite this being a real and growing use case
[MOCK] No clear disclosure of assumptions and limitations, leaving readers unable to judge how much to trust the figures given
differentiation_opportunities: Build the article around three explicitly labeled, internally consistent scenarios (pessimistic, base case, optimistic) with every weekly, monthly, and annual figure traceable back to stated assumptions — something typical ranking content never does
Clearly separate 'time to pay back the machine' from 'ongoing net profit after payback,' framed as two distinct, clearly labeled outputs of the same model
Anchor the entire model to one real, checkable list price so the reader can substitute their own venue's numbers and re-run the math themselves rather than trusting an opaque average
Explicitly state which scenario is most probable and should be used for planning purposes, rather than presenting a false sense of equal likelihood across outcomes
Speak directly to the affluent host-who-also-runs-a-venue persona (lake house, event barn, private bar) that generic operator-forum and vendor content ignores entirely
Add a dedicated assumptions-and-limitations section for transparency, which almost never appears in this content category and builds meaningful trust with a skeptical, numbers-first reader
paa_answered: [MOCK] How much money does an arcade machine make in a bar per week? — typically answered, but usually as one unverified blended figure
[MOCK] How is revenue usually split between the bar owner and the machine owner? — typically answered reasonably well in operator-facing content
[MOCK] What ongoing costs and maintenance does an arcade machine in a bar require? — mentioned in passing but rarely quantified
paa_missed: [MOCK] What is considered a good ROI for an arcade machine? — rarely given a concrete, defensible benchmark
[MOCK] How long does it typically take an arcade machine to pay for itself? — usually vague or entirely absent as a distinct calculation
[MOCK] Does an arcade machine make less money in the off-season or in a slow venue? — seasonality and low-traffic scenarios are typically glossed over
[MOCK] How much does electricity cost to run an arcade machine continuously? — almost never quantified in ranking content
[MOCK] Is buying an arcade machine for a bar or event venue actually a good investment? — typically answered with sales-oriented optimism rather than a genuinely weighed, honest assessment
risks_to_avoid: [MOCK] Avoid presenting a single average earnings figure as fact the way most vendor and forum content does — it undermines credibility with a numbers-first reader
[MOCK] Avoid vendor-style enthusiasm ('easy passive income') that typical sales pages lean on, which reads as untrustworthy to a skeptical operator-minded audience
[MOCK] Avoid burying or omitting maintenance and electricity costs the way most ranking content does — subtracting them is exactly where this article can outperform typical results
[MOCK] Avoid treating best-case anecdotal earnings as typical, a common distortion in operator-forum-style content
[MOCK] Avoid gamer or hype-driven language; typical arcade content skews toward enthusiast tone, which conflicts with the grounded business-analysis voice this brief requires
notes_for_writer: Lead with the three-scenario model early and keep it the structural spine of the article; typical competitor content buries or omits this entirely, so it is the clearest differentiation lever available

Show every calculation step (weekly → monthly → annual, revenue minus revenue-split minus electricity minus maintenance) so a skeptical reader can verify the math themselves — this is the single biggest gap in existing content
Explicitly state that the base case is the one to plan around and that pessimistic/optimistic are not equally probable, per the brief's risk requirements
Include a distinct, clearly separated section on post-payback net monthly profit — do not let it blend into the payback-period discussion
Add an assumptions-and-limitations disclosure near the end; this is rare in this content category and will build trust with the target persona

Keep the JVL ECHO Commercial Edition mention to one soft, honest section near the end, and be explicit that the venue context requires the Commercial (bill/coin acceptor) SKU versus the Home Edition, per the claims-to-verify constraints
